newsitem.title: BELGIUM: SOCCER-BOSMAN MATCH MAY FIND A HOME IN BRUSSELS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-BOSMAN MATCH MAY FIND A HOME IN BRUSSELS.

text.p: The football match that no-one appears to want could finally go ahead in Brussels -- but when it takes place is anyone's guess.

The benefit in aid of Belgian Jean-Marc Bosman which had been repeatedly blocked by one soccer authority or another in the past year, is now likely to go ahead in Brussels, organisers the International soccer Players' Union (AIFP) said on Monday.

"I cannot confirm it as yet...but it is very likely it will be in Brussels," AIFP Secretary-General Didier Roustan told reporters after the union's first meeting with European Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn.
He was unable to give a date or further details on the match, the venue and date of which has been changed several times.

Last year the Spanish F.A. vetoed the match being staged in Spain, but the AIFP, which was represented at the meeting with Flynn by Manchester United's French skipper Eric Cantona, PSG's Brazilian Rai and Belgian Georges Grun of Reggiana, said they are still planning to organise a game in Barcelona on April 27 between a "European" team and a "Rest of the World" team.
With more than 20 World Cup qualifiers scheduled for Wedenesday April 30, the make-up of those teams is unlikely to include any current world-ranked stars.
Roustan said the AIFP would also organise a match in support of the European year against racism later in the year.
Cantona confirmed he would be "very proud" to play in the anti-racism game.
Bosman's case in the European Court of Justice brought about the end of quotas on foreign players in Europe, but also left the player financially stranded after a five-year legal fight.
Cantona said soccer was "at a turning point" now that the Bosman ruling had been accepted by soccer authorities.
He said that now more and more soccer-related cases were brought to court.

"We feel that we're going to have a need for some sort of legal framework. This is going to come in the near future, laws will be created and we would like to fully participate in that process of creating laws," he said.
Flynn said the players had immediately shown their concern and expressed their support for the European year against racism.
"I hadn't expected such a generous response," he said.
He said that AIFP wanted to be involved in soccer-related issues at the highest level.
"They want to be consulted and they want to have a say in how a game is organised in the best interest of the game," he said.
"We've agreed that this will not be the only occasion to meet to discuss further possibilities in so far as the progress of football is concerned," he said.
Dutch Euro MP Jimmy Janssen van Raay said he had always supported the idea of an international trade union of players.
"That way players with a world-wide fame could take care of lesser-known colleagues," he said.
